title: Find Peak Element
description:
# Find Peak Element

A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than each existing neighbor.

Given a **0-indexed** integer array `nums`, return the index of any peak element. If the array contains more than one peak, returning any valid peak index is allowed.

You may imagine that `nums[-1]` and `nums[nums.length]` are both negative infinity, so the first or last element can be a peak when it is greater than its only real neighbor.

Use `O(log n)` time, where `n` is the array length.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,1]

**Output:** 2

**Explanation:** `nums[2] = 3` is greater than both neighbors.

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [1,2,1,3,5,6,4]

**Output:** 5

**Explanation:** Both index 1 and index 5 are peaks; this official test expects index 5.

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 1000`
* `-2147483648 <= nums[i] <= 2147483647`
* `nums[i] != nums[i + 1]` for every valid `i`.

tests.description: Multiple peaks with the expected answer on the right
Increasing pair peaks at the end
Decreasing pair peaks at the beginning
Strictly increasing array peaks at the last index
Strictly decreasing array peaks at the first index
Multiple peaks with the expected answer in the right half
Negative values near the lower integer bound
Two peaks with the chosen answer after the valley

solutions.name: Half-Open Slope Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Binary search by comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`. If the slope rises, a peak must exist to the right. Otherwise, `mid` itself or some index to its left is a peak.

## Key Insight

Moving uphill must eventually end at a peak because the virtual value outside the array is negative infinity. The slope comparison preserves a search interval that always contains at least one peak.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Closed Interval with Neighbor Predicate
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a closed interval and explicitly check whether `mid` is greater than its real neighbors. Missing neighbors are treated as negative infinity. If `mid` is not a peak, follow the side whose neighbor is larger.

## Key Insight

When a neighbor is larger than `mid`, walking in that direction must reach some peak. This turns the local neighbor comparison into a valid half-discarding rule.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Candidate Answer Slope Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep `answer` as the best index seen on a falling slope. When the midpoint rises to the right, discard the left side. When the midpoint falls, record `mid` and keep searching left, because `mid` may be a peak.

## Key Insight

This is the same slope invariant with an explicit candidate variable. It is useful for teaching why a falling midpoint cannot be thrown away.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Slope Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Apply the same slope rule recursively. A rising midpoint sends the search to `[mid + 1, right]`; a falling midpoint keeps `mid` and searches `[left, mid]`. The base case returns the only remaining index.

## Key Insight

Every recursive call keeps an interval that contains at least one peak. This makes the existence proof explicit while preserving logarithmic time.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
